items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: In Springfield Frankie Newton and I were room mates.

ctx.x: From then on, Louis Armstrong was my dominant influence, and no-one in any orchestra that I ever heard enthused me as much. I thought it was the most wonderful sound I had ever heard on any instrument, because he sounded so different from everybody else in the whole band. He was like a star shinning on a stormy night. I started to buy Armstrong records - this was after he had left Fletcher Henderson and had returned to Chicago to record on his own. I remember I bought "Wild Man Blues" and learnt to play the solo…

In those days, we did not have musical papers, and only a few of the guys bought records. The recording of "Money Blues" with Armstrong's solo on it, was the first Fletcher Henderson recording I had heard. Perhaps that is why there were quite a lot of players who were not influenced by Louis Armstrong; For instance, the trumpet player Frankie Newton, who joined Lloyd Scott's orchestra the same time as I, was more influenced by Bix Beidebeck, as was another trumpet player, whose name was Hicks, who was in the band…

I enjoyed Fletcher's band and eventually found out the names of the musicians and especially the soloists such as Charlie "Big" Green, trombone. Joe Smith and Armstrong, Buster Bailey, and Coleman Hawkins-who was the tenor sax and bass saxophone player that could swing a band into bad health. You could hear his sax cutting through when the whole band was giving everything they had ensemble.
